summary: Cape St. Francis Lighthouse, southern entrance to Conception Bay: first lit 1877 with a red light; now a lantern on a 1957 concrete building, listed unstaffed (2005 DFO), tower closed.

structures.note: Short square tower on the flat roof of the wooden dwelling, carrying the first lantern (LighthouseFriends). The 1877 light had its focal plane at 37.5 m; replaced in 1957
Two-storey keepers' duplex (LighthouseFriends); demolished 1993 for a helicopter pad (LighthouseFriends and Rowlett; nllh3d gives 1997)
Octagonal lantern house on a rectangular concrete fog-signal building (Coast Guard list; LighthouseFriends, Rowlett)

staffing.note: Listed as unstaffed in the Fisheries and Oceans Canada brochure DFO/2005-167 (copyright 2005). The Fisheries and Oceans web page reads 'Date modified: 2019-09-24', a web-page date. Last resident keeper left in 1975 (LighthouseFriends)

access.note: Grounds open; the building is fenced and the tower is closed. Reached by a 5.5 km hiking path from Pouch Cove (Rowlett); the road beyond Pouch Cove is unpaved (LighthouseFriends). Owned by the Canadian Coast Guard.

events.note: An Act for the erection of a light house on or near Cape St Francis passed on 25 April 1872 (LighthouseFriends)
Schooner Village Belle lost at Cape St. Francis on 30 July 1872 (Northern Maritime Research list). Before the light
Construction began in 1876 (launchway at Biscayne Cove, contract to Cameron & Carnell); first light January 1877
First lit 10 January 1877: fixed red light from a fifth-order lens, focal plane 37.5 m (LighthouseFriends). Rowlett gives station established 1877
Coal-fired steam siren fog alarm, made by A. & F. Brown of England, commissioned later in 1877 (LighthouseFriends)
Larger lens and lamp installed in response to complaints that the light was poor (LighthouseFriends)
New optical apparatus; light changed from fixed red to fixed white (LighthouseFriends)
New diaphone fog alarm, a two-and-a-half-second blast each minute (LighthouseFriends)
Original lighthouse replaced by a two-storey keepers' duplex and a concrete fog-signal building topped by a lantern (LighthouseFriends; Rowlett; nllh3d)
Last resident keeper left the station (LighthouseFriends)
Keepers' duplex demolished and a helicopter pad put in its place (LighthouseFriends; Rowlett). nllh3d gives 1997

corrections.proposed: tower, built 1957, 3.3 m, standing; the 1877 tower is lost
corrections.why: The standing lantern house and concrete fog-signal building date from 1957 (LighthouseFriends; Rowlett; nllh3d). The 1877 tower was replaced. The Coast Guard list gives the structure height as 3.3 m.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: 1877 is the first light (LighthouseFriends; Rowlett 'station established 1877'; nllh3d 'finished in 1877'). The record's 1957 date is for the replacement duplex and lantern house, which replaced the 1877 station. A 1878 first-light date found in a web search belongs to a different Cape St Francis in South Africa and does not apply here.

notes_for_editor: Built almost entirely on LighthouseFriends, which cites the Journal of the House of Assembly of Newfoundland and the Evening Telegram (1905). Neither was read directly: the House journals are on MUN's Digital Archives and were not searched; the 1905 Morris account is known only as LighthouseFriends quotes it. The Canadian Marine reports in the corpus do not cover Newfoundland lights (the corpus lists Cape Race and Cape Ray only). Conflicts left open: duplex demolition 1993 (LighthouseFriends, Rowlett) against 1997 (nllh3d); range 16 nm (Coast Guard list) against 15 nmi (nllh3d; Wikipedia infobox). The LighthouseFriends passage spells the inspector 'Neville' in 1879 and 'Nevill' elsewhere; the story uses Nevill. The LighthouseFriends passage on the surprise inspection gives '13 December' with no year; the story says in brackets that no year is printed and does not supply one. The LighthouseFriends roster gives 1964-1968 for both Edward and Franklyn Noseworthy as one span. Rowlett's trail is 'Biscan Cove Path' while LighthouseFriends names Biscayne Cove for the 1876 landing; both are reproduced as their sources give them. Wikipedia's Cape St. Francis (NL) article was read for leads only, and not cited. A web search returned stfrancistoday.com, which describes a different Cape St Francis (South Africa). It was not used. The record's 'Parks Canada' status: the cached Parks Canada heritage-lighthouse list had no match (the cache may be truncated). The unstaffed status is from the Fisheries and Oceans Canada brochure DFO/2005-167 (copyright 2005); its web page reads 'Date modified: 2019-09-24', a web-page date, so the status is dated 2005 and no source read gives current staffing. The 3.3 m structure height is from the Coast Guard list only; Rowlett gives no structure height, so the story no longer cites Rowlett for it.
